findings.title: Device ID is cached before checking the device limit, allowing any repeat request to bypass the limit
findings.body: In `tagDeviceUI`, `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` (line 87) is executed before calling `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(ctx, device)` (line 93), and the cache entry is not removed when `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns an error. When the device limit has been reached, the first request from a new anonymous device will fail with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but its device ID is now stored in `localCache` for 29 minutes. Every subsequent request from that same device hits `if _, ok := a.localCache.Get(key); ok { return nil }` on line 83, causing `TagDevice` to return `nil` and `Anonymous.Authenticate` to succeed. Only the cache entry after `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds (or delete the cache entry on error).

findings.title: MySQL RowsAffected() returns 0 when updated values are unchanged, falsely triggering ErrDeviceLimitReached
findings.body: In `updateDevice`, `result.RowsAffected()` is checked for `== 0` to determine whether the device existed within the active 30-day window, and if 0, `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned. On MySQL (when `clientFoundRows` is not enabled in the DSN) and SQLite/Postgres in certain configurations or rapid requests within the same second (since MySQL `DATETIME` / timestamp columns have 1-second resolution), an `UPDATE` where `client_ip`, `user_agent`, and `updated_at` match the existing row values reports `0` affected rows even though the row matched the `WHERE` clause. When the device limit is reached, an existing valid device making another request within the same second on MySQL will get `0` rows affected and be wrongly rejected with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.
